- **Algorithm (exact step-by-step procedure)** [`algorithm_concept`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/algorithm_concept.md) — K3, use partial, make easy, accept high. Reckoning books, the Easter computus and gunners' tables are step-by-step rules. Nobody treats a procedure as an object to be compared, proved or handed to a machine. Local: reckoning masters; Hofkammer clerks; Jesuit mathematics lessons.
- **Binary numbers** [`binary_numbers`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/binary_numbers.md) — K1, use none, make easy, accept low. Caramuel printed number systems to other bases, binary included (1670). Leibniz's binary manuscript of 1679 is unpublished. It looks like a game with no use. Elsewhere: Hanover: Leibniz.
- **Boolean logic (algebra of true and false)** [`boolean_logic`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/boolean_logic.md) — K1, use none, make easy, accept low. The Jesuit faculty drills Aristotelian syllogisms in Latin. Reasoning by calculation is Leibniz's private dream and Lull's combinatory wheels; schoolmen will see no need for it. Local: Jesuit professors of logic; Kircher, Ars magna sciendi (1669), dedicated to Leopold I. Elsewhere: Hanover: Leibniz's unpublished logical calculus.
- **Switching circuits and logic gates** [`logic_gates_switching`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/logic_gates_switching.md) — K0, use none, make very-hard, accept low
- **Mechanical calculator** [`mechanical_calculator`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/mechanical_calculator.md) — K2, use none, make hard, accept high. Napier's rods are known through Schott's Organum mathematicum, the chest Kircher devised in 1661 for Archduke Karl Joseph. Pascal's adder is a rarity; Leibniz's four-function machine is unfinished. Local: Schott, Organum mathematicum (1668); Vienna and Augsburg clockmakers; Hofkammer and war-chest accounts as customers. Elsewhere: Hanover: Leibniz, stepped reckoner (model shown in London 1673); Paris: surviving Pascal machines; London: Samuel Morland's machines.
- **Punched cards for control and data** [`punched_card_control`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/punched_card_control.md) — K1, use none, make medium, accept medium. The pinned barrel that plays a carillon or automaton organ is familiar, and Kircher prints how to pin a tune. Exchangeable cards steering a loom are unknown. Local: Kircher, Musurgia universalis (1650); Augsburg automaton makers.

A pen-and-paper idea with no audience: the question 'what can a rule-following clerk compute at all' has not been asked. Leibniz would understand it at once. Elsewhere: Hanover: Leibniz.

Millers' hoppers that feed by the stone's speed, float valves and Drebbel's self-regulating furnace are known as separate tricks, with no general idea behind them. Local: millers; alchemists' and assayers' furnaces.
- **Cryptography and codebreaking (ciphers, frequency analysis, one-time pad)** [`cryptography`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/cryptography.md) — K3, use partial, make easy, accept high. Court and field chanceries use number ciphers with code lists; siege letters go out enciphered. Keyword ciphers are thought unbreakable. A captured courier yields the text, rarely the key. Local: Hofkanzlei and Hofkriegsrat cipher clerks; Kircher, Polygraphia nova (1663); Schott, Schola steganographica (1665). Elsewhere: Oxford: John Wallis, the best codebreaker alive; Versailles: the Rossignol family.
- **Public-key cryptography and digital signatures** [`public_key_cryptography`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/public_key_cryptography.md) — K0, use none, make hard, accept low. Fermat's little theorem is in print but nobody can multiply and test large primes fast enough by hand to make it practical.
